summary: Defines a YANG data model for the rules used by Static Context Header Compression and fragmentation. This makes it easier for different SCHC instances to exchange rule sets or change rule parameters in an interoperable way.

plainLanguage.summary: SCHC is a way to shrink the headers of packets sent by small devices, using a rule book that both ends of the link share. RFC 8724 describes that rule book in prose and tables. This document writes it down in a machine-readable format, using the YANG language for network data models, so that two devices can exchange the rules or change one setting in them.

questions: how to exchange schc compression rules
what is a yang data model for schc
how are schc fragmentation rules described
subtitle: A YANG data model that writes down the SCHC compression and fragmentation rules so two devices can share them.

tldr.problem: SCHC compresses and fragments packets on constrained networks using a shared set of Rules, but RFC 8724 describes those Rules only informally. Two ends cannot reliably exchange or edit them from that description.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9363 defines a YANG module, ietf-schc, that describes compression Rules and fragmentation Rules with the same fields and identifiers on both ends, including the field identifier, length, position, direction, target value, matching operator and compression action.
tldr.outcome: Two SCHC instances can now describe the same Rules identically, send a full set of Rules to each other, or change one value such as an IPv6 prefix. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 9441.

today: RFC 9363 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2023, and it is updated by RFC 9441. It defines the YANG module ietf-schc for the SCHC framework of RFC 8724.

sections.title: Why SCHC Rules Need a Data Model
sections.content:
SCHC (Static Context Header Compression) is a compression and fragmentation mechanism for constrained networks, defined in RFC 8724. It is based on a static context shared by two entities at the boundary of the constrained network. RFC 8724 provides an informal representation of the Rules used either for compression and decompression (C/D) or for fragmentation and reassembly (F/R).

The goal of this document is to formalize the description of the Rules, so that there is the same definition on both ends even if the internal representation is different, and so that one end can be updated to set up specific values, for example an IPv6 prefix or a destination address. The document [LPWAN-ARCH] illustrates the exchange of Rules using the YANG data model.

This document defines a YANG data model, as defined in RFC 7950, to represent both compression and fragmentation Rules. That leads to a common representation for the values of all the elements of a Rule.
sections.plainLanguage: Two devices that compress packets together must agree on the rules they use. The rules were only described in prose, so this document gives them a fixed machine-readable form that both devices can read.

sections.title: The Terms the Model Uses
sections.content:
The terminology extends that of RFC 8376, the Low-Power Wide Area Network overview. The abbreviations used throughout the model are:

  • App: a Low-Power WAN application that sends packets to or receives packets from the device.
  • Dev: the device, as defined in RFC 8376.
  • Context: the set of Rules used to compress and decompress headers.
  • FID: the Field Identifier, which identifies the protocol and the field a Field Descriptor applies to.
  • FL: the Field Length, the length of the original packet header field, given in bits for fixed-length fields or as a type such as variable or token length when the length is unknown when the Rule is created.
  • FP: the Field Position, which selects which occurrence of a repeated field the descriptor applies to, counting from 1. The value 0 is special and means don't care.
  • DI: the Direction Indicator, telling whether the descriptor applies to packets travelling Up, Dw or Bi, which allows asymmetric processing with the same Rule.
  • TV: the Target Value, a value contained in a Rule that is matched against the value of a header field.
  • MO: the Matching Operator, used to match a value in a header field with a value in a Rule.
  • CDA: the Compression/Decompression Action, the pair of actions performed at the compressor to compress a header field and at the decompressor to recover the original value.
  • RuleID: the Rule Identifier. The SCHC C/D on both sides shares the same RuleID for a given packet.
  • L2 Word: the minimum subdivision of payload data that the Layer 2 will carry. In most Layer 2 technologies it is an octet; in bit-oriented radio technologies it might be a single bit.

The direction terms are defined in the document: Up is the uplink direction, from the device's SCHC C/D to the network's SCHC C/D, and Dw is the downlink direction, from the network's SCHC C/D to the device's SCHC C/D.
sections.plainLanguage: The model uses short names for the parts of a rule. Each name says what it is: which field of the header, how long that field is, which direction it travels in, what value to compare it against, and what to do with it afterwards.

sections.title: How the Identifiers and Naming Conventions Work
sections.content:
The identifiers used in the SCHC YANG data model come from the identityref statement, to ensure global uniqueness and easy augmentation if needed. The principle for defining a new type based on a group of identityref is: define a main identity ending with the keyword base-type, derive all the identities used in the data model from this base type, and create a typedef from that base type. The document shows this with the Reassembly Check Sequence (RCS) algorithms used during SCHC fragmentation, where rcs-crc32 is the CRC32 algorithm defined as the default RCS in RFC 8724 and is 4 bytes long.

Each kind of value then follows a naming convention. A field is named with fid- followed by the protocol name and the field name, and each field MUST be identified through a global YANG identityref derived from fid-base-type. An identity for each protocol is specified using fid-<protocol name>-base-type, and all possible fields for that protocol MUST derive from the protocol identity. If a field has to be divided into subfields, the field identity serves as a base. The current data model includes the field definitions found in RFC 8724 and RFC 8824.

The Field Length is either an integer giving the size of a field in bits or a specific function. RFC 8724 defines the var function for variable-length fields, and RFC 8824 defines the tkl function for the CoAP Token Length field. The convention is fl- followed by the function name, and the type is a union between an integer giving the size in bits and the identityref. The Field Position is a positive integer, of type uint8, whose default value is 1 and which is incremented at each repetition; the value 0 indicates that the position is not important and is not considered during the Rule selection process. The Direction Indicator uses the convention di followed by the indicator name, and its type is di-type.

The Target Value is a list of binary sequences of any length, aligned to the left, used in the Rule as a list with the index as a key. The highest index value is used to compute the size of the index sent in residue for the match-mapping CDA. For equal and most significant bits (MSBs) the Target Value contains a single element, so the index is set to 0. For match-mapping it can contain several elements, and index values MUST start from 0 and MUST be contiguous. If the header field contains text, the binary sequence uses the same encoding.

The Matching Operator is a function applied between a field value provided by the parsed header and the Target Value. RFC 8724 defines 4 matching operators, the convention is mo- followed by the operator name, and the type is mo-type. The Compression/Decompression Action identifies the function to use for compression or decompression; RFC 8724 defines 7 such actions, the convention is cda- followed by the action name, and the type is cda-type. Currently no CDA requires arguments, but some may require one or several in the future, viewed as a list of target-value type.
sections.plainLanguage: Every value in the rule book has a globally unique name built from a fixed prefix, such as mo- for a matching operator. Because the names are unique across the Internet, two devices cannot describe different things with the same word.

sections.title: The Fragmentation Rule and the Fragment Header
sections.content:
Fragmentation is optional in the data model and depends on the presence of the fragmentation feature. Most of the fragmentation parameters are listed in Appendix D of RFC 8724. Since fragmentation Rules work for a specific direction, they MUST contain a mandatory Direction Indicator; the type is the same as the one used in compression entries, but bidirectional MUST NOT be used.

RFC 8724 defines 3 fragmentation modes. In No ACK the mode is unidirectional and no acknowledgment is sent back. In ACK Always each fragmentation window must be explicitly acknowledged before going to the next. In ACK on Error a window is acknowledged only when the receiver detects some missing fragments. The type is fragmentation-mode-type, with the convention fragmentation-mode- followed by the mode name.

A data fragment header, starting with the RuleID, can be sent in the fragmentation direction. The RFC indicates that the SCHC header may be composed of the following:

  • A Datagram Tag (DTag) identifying the datagram being fragmented if the fragmentation applies concurrently on several datagrams. This field is optional, and its length is defined by the Rule.
  • A Window (W) used in ACK-Always and ACK-on-Error modes. In ACK-Always its size is 1, and in ACK-on-Error it depends on the Rule. This field is not needed in No-ACK mode.
  • A Fragment Compressed Number (FCN) indicating the fragment or tile position within the window. This field is mandatory in all modes defined in RFC 8724, and its size is defined by the Rule.

The last fragment of a datagram is sent with a Reassembly Check Sequence (RCS) field, to detect residual transmission errors and possible losses in the last window. RFC 8724 defines a single algorithm based on Ethernet CRC computation, and the convention is rcs- followed by the algorithm name. For ACK-on-Error mode, the All-1 fragment may just contain the RCS or can include a tile, and the parameters define the behaviour: all-1-data-no means the last fragment contains no data, just the RCS; all-1-data-yes means it includes a single tile and the RCS; and all-1-data-sender-choice means it may or may not contain a single tile, and the receiver can detect if a tile is present.

The acknowledgment fragment header goes in the opposite direction to the data. It is composed of a DTag if present, a mandatory window as in the data fragment, and a C bit giving the status of RCS validation; in case of failure a bitmap follows, indicating the received tile. For ACK-on-Error, SCHC defines when an acknowledgment can be sent: at any time defined by the Layer 2, at the end of a window (FCN all-0), or as a response to receiving the last fragment (FCN all-1). The convention is ack-behavior followed by the algorithm name.
sections.plainLanguage: When a message is too large for one packet, the rules say how to cut it up. Each piece carries a number saying where it belongs, and the last piece carries a check value so the receiver can tell whether anything was lost.

sections.title: Timers, Retries and Layer 2 Settings
sections.content:
The state machine of fragmentation needs some common values to handle fragmentation correctly.

  • The Retransmission Timer gives the duration before sending an ACK request. If specified, the value MUST be strictly positive.
  • The Inactivity Timer gives the duration before aborting a fragmentation session. The value 0 explicitly indicates that this timer is disabled.

RFC 8724 does not specify any range for these timers, and RFC 9011 recommends a duration of 12 hours. The value range should be between milliseconds for real-time systems and several days for worse-than-best-effort systems. To allow a large range of applications, two parameters must be specified. The first is the duration of a tick, computed by the formula 2^(tick-duration)/10^6. When tick-duration is set to 0, the unit is the microsecond; the default value of 20 leads to a unit of 1.048575 seconds, and a value of 32 leads to a tick-duration of about 1 hour 11 minutes. The second is the number of ticks in the predefined unit: with the default tick-duration value of 20, the timers can cover a range between 1.0 second and 19 hours, as recommended in RFC 9011.

The fragmentation protocol also specifies the number of attempts before aborting, through the parameter max-ack-requests. The data model includes two Layer 2 parameters. The l2-word-size gives the base fragmentation, in bits, on a Layer 2 Word that can be of any length; the default value is 8 and corresponds to the default value for the byte-aligned Layer 2, and a value of 1 indicates that there is no alignment and no need for padding. The maximum-packet-size defines the maximum size of an uncompressed datagram, and by default the value is set to 1280 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules also carry the timings: how long to wait before asking again for a missing piece, and how long to wait before giving up. A tick is the unit these timers are counted in, so one pair of numbers can cover anything from a second to about 19 hours.

sections.title: How a Rule Is Defined in the Model
sections.content:
A Rule is identified by a unique Rule Identifier comprising both a RuleID value and a RuleID length, and the YANG grouping rule-id-type defines the structure used to represent a RuleID. A length of 0 is allowed, to represent an implicit Rule. Three natures of Rules are defined in RFC 8724, and the data model introduces one identity for each:

  • Compression: a compression Rule is associated with the RuleID.
  • No-compression: this identifies the default Rule used to send a packet integrally when no compression Rule was found.
  • Fragmentation: fragmentation parameters are associated with the RuleID. Fragmentation is optional, and the feature fragmentation should be set.

The naming convention is nature- followed by the nature identifier. To access a specific Rule, the RuleID length and value are used as a key.

A compression Rule is composed of entries describing its processing, and an entry contains all the information defined in the figure of RFC 8724: the Field ID, the Field Length, the Field Position, the Direction Indicator, the Target Value, the Matching Operator and the Compression/Decompression Action. The compression-content grouping defines a list of compression-rule-entry, indexed by their Field ID, position and direction. Some checks are performed on the values: when the Matching Operator is ignore, no Target Value is needed, but for other matching operators there MUST be a Target Value present, and when the MSB matching operator is specified, the matching-operator-value must be present.

The data model conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture of RFC 8342. Its top level is a schc container holding a list of rule entries keyed by rule-id-value and rule-id-length, with either a compression subtree or a fragmentation subtree inside each entry.

IANA registered the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-schc in the IETF XML Registry, with the IESG as registrant contact. The YANG data model was registered in the YANG Module Names registry with the name ietf-schc, the prefix schc and RFC 9363 as the reference. The module file in the document is named ietf-schc@2023-03-01.yang.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule is found by its number and the length of that number. Each rule is either a compression rule, a fragmentation rule, or the rule that says to send the packet untouched. The rules are stored in one list, so a device can be sent the whole list at once.

sections.title: The Worked Example
sections.content:
The appendix takes three informal Rules and writes them out in XML using the model. Rule 6/3 is a compression Rule for IPv6 headers, and the XML shows one entry per header field. The IPv6 version field is 4 bits, bidirectional, matched with mo-equal against 6 and handled with cda-not-sent, so it costs nothing on the wire. The payload length is ignored by matching and recomputed with cda-compute, and the application prefix and interface identifier are sent as values with cda-value-sent.

Rule 12/11 is a fragmentation Rule in No ACK mode with a DTag of 2 bits, a window of 0 bits and an FCN of 3 bits, using the CRC32 RCS algorithm, and Rule 100/8 is a no-compression Rule.

The XML uses the same names as the model: rule-id-value and rule-id-length for the identifier, rule-nature for the kind of rule, and one entry per header field, each holding field-id, field-length, field-position, direction-indicator, target-value, matching-operator and comp-decomp-action.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows one real rule written in the format, with a line for each part of the IPv6 header. Some lines say not to send the value at all, because both ends already know it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The YANG module defines a schema for data that is designed to be accessed via network management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. The lowest NETCONF layer is the secure transport layer, where the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH, and the lowest RESTCONF layer is HTTPS, where the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is TLS. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) provides the means to restrict access for particular NETCONF or RESTCONF users to a preconfigured subset of the available protocol operations and content.

A number of data nodes in the module are writable, creatable or deletable, and they may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. Write operations to these data nodes without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. All the data nodes under /schc may be modified. The Rule contains sensitive information, such as the application IPv6 address where the device's data will be sent after decompression. An attacker may try to modify other devices' Rules by changing the application address, and may block communication or allow traffic eavesdropping. Therefore a device must be allowed to modify only its own rules on the remote SCHC instance, and the identity of the requester must be validated, which can be done through certificates or access lists. Modification may be allowed regarding the Field Descriptor: IPv6 address descriptors should not be modified, but a UDP device port could be changed.

Some of the readable data nodes may also be considered sensitive. It is thus important to control read access, for example through get, get-config or notification operations. By reading a module, an attacker may learn the traffic generated by a device and can also learn about application addresses or the REST API.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say where a device's data goes after it is decompressed. Someone who can change them can redirect that data, so only the owner should be allowed to change a device's own rules, and the reader should be checked. The same applies to reading the rules, because they reveal what the device sends.

viz.caption: THE ABBREVIATIONS USED BY THE MODEL

items.title: FID, FL, FP
items.text: Which header field, how long it is, and which occurrence of it.

items.title: DI
items.text: Direction Indicator: Up, Dw or Bi.

items.title: TV
items.text: Target Value: the value the field is compared against.

items.title: MO
items.text: Matching Operator: how the field and the Target Value are compared.

items.title: CDA
items.text: Compression/Decompression Action: what is done to the field.

items.title: RuleID
items.text: The number that names one rule on both ends of the link.

items.title: L2 Word
items.text: The smallest piece of payload the Layer 2 carries.

items.title: App, Dev, Context
items.text: The application, the device, and the shared set of rules.
